newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.African rand at all-time low vs dollar.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.African rand at all-time low vs dollar.

text.p: The South African rand plunged below 4.60 to the dollar for the first time on Friday, hit by downbeat comments from central bank governor Chris Stals.

Stals warned that already high South African interest rates might have to be raised further if there was no slowdown in money supply growth, and cautioned that the country's low reserves ruled out any early scrapping of exchange controls on residents.
That took its toll on the bond market and prompted heavy selling of the currency, particularly by overseas investors, dealers said.
The central Reserve Bank stepped in around midday to steady the rand but it remained on the ropes, touching a low of 4.6150/6200 from 4.5840/5890 on Thursday.
The rand has now lost over 25 percent of its value against the dollar since mid-February, and some 20 percent versus a basket of currencies of South Africa's major trading partners.
Stals and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, both addressing an economic conference here, said they believed the unit was now stabilising.
But dealers and chartists, who predict prices from historical trends, were sceptical -- especially in view of the limited reserves available to the central bank.

South Africa's foreign reserves have been halved in dollar terms since the end of 1995, falling from 15.7 billion rand ($4.3 billion at the prevailing rates) to 10.0 billion rand at the end of September ($2.2 billion), equivalent to just four weeks import cover.
Stals said that the low level of reserves ruled out any immediate lifting of exchange controls on residents.
Allowing residents to invest abroad meant there had to be a reasonable assurance that it would be possible to convert rand assets into foreign currencies, he said.
"With its low level of foreign reserves, the Reserve Bank cannot provide this assurance. In our situation, to act precipitately could create disaster," Stals said.
He criticised commentators who suggested South Africa would abolish all remaining controls in a "big bang" approach, saying this was creating false expectations and unnecessary fears.
South Africans, who have long waited for the restrictions to be lifted, currently only can get foreign currency -- and then limited amounts -- when they travel abroad.
President Nelson Mandela's government has committed itself to the eventual scrapping of controls on the rand, but the lack of a timetable has frustrated investors.

Stals threw further cold water over financial markets by warning the central bank might need to raise already high interest rates if there was no sign of a slowdown in bank credit extension and money supply growth.
Stals said there was evidence money growth had started to level out at a relatively high level but the central bank was growing impatient for signs of an actual fall.
"Up to now, the monetary authorities were prepared to be tolerant, and to wait for further signals of an actual decline in the growth rates of these important anchors for monetary policy," he said.
"Should new statistics contradict this assumption, there will be no alternative but to tighten monetary policy further."
Commercial banks' prime lending rate currently stands at 19.25 percent. The Bank rate is fixed at 16.00 percent.
